long.vo: New Zealand were bowled out for one hundred and thirty-four. India then slumped to one hundred and thirteen for seven in the chase, and still won by four runs, without finishing it. Here's how the second ODI in Wellington really played out.

Rain threatened all day, so the match was cut to forty-seven overs a side. शुभमन गिल won the toss and bowled first. The pitch had pace, bounce and moisture. Mitchell Santner later called it a tricky surface, with nowhere to hide.

India's plan came straight from Gurnoor Brar. In India, he said, the pitches are flat and you live on the hard length. In New Zealand, the extra bounce rewards a bowler who attacks. So India stacked the slip cordon and hit that length, again and again.

scene.sub: Four catchers behind the bat. Hit the same length. Let the bounce do the rest.

long.vo: It worked. Auqib Nabi removed Will Young and Tim Seifert early. Then, in the twentieth over, Brar struck twice, Tom Latham and Glenn Phillips, and New Zealand were fifty-three for five. Daryl Mitchell fought back with fifty-five, and Santner added thirty-one. But New Zealand were all out for one thirty-four in forty-one overs, their lowest all-out total against India in a home ODI.

events.t: All out in 41 overs: NZ's lowest at home vs India

long.vo: Brar finished with four for thirty and the player of the match award. Anshul Kamboj took two for twenty-five, and Nabi two for thirty-one.

tiles.l: GURNOOR BRAR · PLAYER OF THE MATCH

long.vo: A target of one thirty-five should have been easy. But New Zealand had the same weapon. Jacob Duffy pitched it up with a full slip cordon, bowled शुभमन गिल first ball, and removed विराट कोहली for seven. India were seventeen for two.

scene.sub: Gill bowled first ball. Kohli gone for 7.

long.vo: Then Kyle Jamieson took over. At six foot eight, he's built for a pitch like this. He worked over रोहित शर्मा before getting him caught for twenty-three. He got श्रेयस अय्यर with a short ball that seamed in and took the edge through to the keeper. And later, Kamboj top-edged him to deep third.

head.sub: THE BOUNCER FROM SIX FOOT EIGHT

scene.sub: Rohit, Iyer and Kamboj: all to Jamieson.

long.vo: From there, India kept losing wickets. Four for one. Seventeen for two. Thirty-nine for three. Forty-seven for four. Then Iyer at eighty-six, Naman Dhir at one hundred and eight, and Kamboj at one hundred and eleven.

And then the rain came. After twenty-six overs, India were one thirteen for seven. The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern par score at that moment was one hundred and nine. India were four runs ahead, and play never resumed.

So how does that par work? DLS treats a chase as two resources: overs left, and wickets in hand. Lose wickets, and your par score rises fast. That's why seven down was so dangerous. One more wicket before the rain, and India would almost certainly have been behind par.

items.d: Overs remaining AND wickets in hand
Each one pushes the par score up
India were 4 ahead, with almost no cushion
...and they'd likely have been behind par

long.vo: The man who stood still in the chaos was KL Rahul: twenty-six not out off thirty-eight balls. Not glamorous, but without him there was no par to beat.

Our verdict? India's bowlers won this match. Their batters nearly gave it away. Even शुभमन गिल admitted they lost a couple more wickets than they'd have liked. And the lesson for the rest of this tour: in New Zealand, the hard length rules.
Would India have chased it without the rain? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more tactical breakdowns.

short.vo: New Zealand made one thirty-four. India slumped to one thirteen for seven, and still won.
India's plan: Gurnoor Brar's hard length, with a packed slip cordon. Four for thirty.
But Kyle Jamieson bounced India out: three for thirty-five.
Then the rain came. India were four runs ahead of the DLS par. One more wicket, and they'd likely have lost.
